original_value: Concerns about climate change associated with the combustion of fossil fuels urge a call for widespread reductions in household energy use. Determining means of achieving this is a key challenge faced by environmental scientists. The current research presents insights gained from a 12-month empirical trial of new serious game for energy, ‘EnergyCat’; which was designed to encourage household energy reductions in the UK social housing sector. Effects of gameplay on consumption behaviours and energy awareness were explored using 82 UK social housing households (versus a no-game control). Results indicated the intervention did not lead to any substantive changes in awareness or consumption practices. However, post-intervention feedback highlighted several issues in terms of game design and usability that may explain why the game failed to change behaviour in this instance. We provide a framework of suggestions as to how the game design process could be improved in order to engage residents in future, including use of adaptive fonts for older residents, and provision of clearer instructions on gameplay objectives at the outset. In addition, researchers should ensure close collaboration is maintained with residents throughout the design process in future efforts, in order to maximise likelihood of ongoing engagement from this population.

result.paraphrase: Climate change concerns linked to fossil-fuel combustion have prompted calls for major reductions in household energy use, and finding effective ways to achieve this remains a central challenge for environmental scientists. This study reports findings from a 12-month empirical trial of a new serious game for energy, EnergyCat, created to encourage lower household energy consumption in the UK social housing sector. Using 82 UK social housing households and a no-game control, the researchers examined how gameplay affected energy awareness and consumption behaviour. The results showed no meaningful change in either awareness or consumption practices. However, post-intervention feedback identified several game-design and usability problems that may help explain why the intervention did not alter behaviour. The paper offers recommendations for improving the design process to better engage residents in future, including adaptive fonts for older residents and clearer instructions about gameplay goals from the outset. It also recommends that future work maintain close collaboration with residents throughout design to maximise the chances of sustained engagement from this group.
